opus-5.5.text:
I think about it at a few different levels.

In the near term, our goal is very concrete: make 3D content creation ten times faster and ten times cheaper for the people who already make 3D — game developers, indie studios, 3D printing hobbyists, product designers, people in film and XR. Today, making a single good-quality game-ready asset can take an artist days. If we can bring that down to minutes, with something that's actually usable in production — clean topology, good textures, rigging, animation — that already changes the economics of a lot of industries.

But the bigger ambition is something I'd describe as democratizing 3D. Think about what happened with 2D. Photography used to be a professional thing, and then smartphones made everyone a photographer. Video used to require expensive equipment, and then TikTok and phones made everyone a video creator. 3D has never had that moment. It's still locked behind tools like Maya, Blender, ZBrush — incredibly powerful, but with a learning curve of years. So the number of people who can actually create 3D content is tiny compared to the number of people who have ideas they'd like to bring into 3D. I'd like Meshy to be the thing that breaks that barrier, so anyone with an idea can turn it into a 3D object.

And then, longer term, I believe 3D is the natural interface to the physical world. We live in 3D. Robots operate in 3D. Simulation, embodied AI, digital twins, manufacturing — they all need a huge amount of 3D content. Back in my PhD days working on Taichi and physical simulation, one of the biggest bottlenecks was always: where does the content come from? You can have the best simulator in the world, but if you don't have the assets, you can't build the worlds. So I see 3D generation as a foundational layer — not just for games and entertainment, but for how AI eventually understands and interacts with the physical world.

So, if I had to put it in one sentence: we want Meshy to become the default way humanity creates 3D content. That's a very long journey, and we're still early, but I think the direction is pretty clear.

r001.rationale: The response describes Meshy’s ambition as becoming the default way to create 3D content; it does not discuss going public or say that doing so would be insufficient.

r002.rationale: It presents 3D generation as a foundation for uses such as simulation and embodied AI, but does not identify accumulated multimodal AI capabilities as the basis for pursuing an opportunity beyond 3D generation.

r003.rationale: The response calls the ambition a long journey and says Meshy is early, but gives no target for identifying a next opportunity before growth slows.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. When I think about the ultimate ambition for Meshy, I don't really think of it as a "3D generation" business in the narrow sense. The way I frame it is: we want to make creating 3D content as easy as writing a sentence or sketching an idea, so that the cost of producing 3D goes down by orders of magnitude, and 3D stops being a bottleneck for anyone who wants to build something.

Right now, 3D is one of the most expensive forms of media to produce. A single game-ready character can take a skilled artist days or weeks of modeling, UV unwrapping, texturing, rigging. That's why 3D has stayed mostly in the hands of studios with big budgets. Games, films, product visualization, that's where the money is, and even there the pipeline is painful. Compare that to text, images, or even video, where the barrier to entry has collapsed in the last few years. 3D is the last big modality where creation is still fundamentally gated by skill and time.

So the first layer of the ambition is very practical: become the tool that every 3D creator, professional or hobbyist, reaches for first. Not to replace artists, but to take care of the ninety percent of the work that is tedious and let people spend their time on the ten percent that is creative. If a game studio can prototype a hundred assets in an afternoon instead of commissioning ten, that changes how they design.

The second layer is bigger. If 3D content becomes cheap and abundant, a lot of things that don't exist today become possible. Games where the world is generated on the fly around what the player wants. Education where a kid can ask for a model of a cell or an engine and actually take it apart. E-commerce where every product has a real 3D representation. And eventually, as AR and VR hardware matures, the spatial computing world is going to need an enormous amount of 3D content that simply can't be produced by hand. Somebody has to build the engine that supplies that.

And the third layer, which is more personal to me coming from a graphics and systems background, is that 3D is really the bridge between AI and the physical world. Images are a projection. 3D is geometry, materials, physics. If you want AI to understand how things are shaped, how they fit together, how they move, you need a strong foundation in 3D. So I think of Meshy as building the infrastructure for that, step by step, starting from where there's real demand today, which is games and content creation.

So, in one line: the ultimate ambition is to make 3D creation accessible to everyone, and in doing so, unlock a whole category of experiences that aren't economically possible right now. We're early, the models still have a long way to go, but the direction is clear.

r001.rationale: The response describes making 3D creation accessible and unlocking new experiences, but does not discuss taking Meshy public or say that doing so would be insufficient.

r002.rationale: It mentions 3D as a foundation for AI to understand the physical world, but does not identify accumulated multimodal AI capabilities as the basis for an opportunity beyond 3D generation.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention identifying a next opportunity beyond 3D or tie that goal to a shift from exponential to slower growth.

astra-6.text: I think the ultimate ambition is to make creating 3D content accessible to everyone. Today, you can have a great idea for a character or a world, but turning that idea into a 3D asset requires specialized skills and a lot of time. We want to close that gap between imagination and creation. For professionals, that means being able to iterate much faster. For someone who has never learned 3D modeling, it means being able to start creating at all. Ultimately, I’d like Meshy to help people spend more time deciding what they want to create and less time figuring out how to make the tools do it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the ultimate ambition is to make creating 3D content as easy as expressing an idea. Today, you can imagine something very clearly, but turning it into a usable 3D asset still requires specialized skills and a lot of time. We want to close that gap.

For Meshy, that means helping professional artists work faster while also opening up creation to people who have never used a 3D tool. Ultimately, I’d love for anyone to be able to build the objects, characters, and worlds they imagine, without the technical process becoming the limiting factor.
